hints: Start at the top of Fig. 6.1 where two blood vessels enter the capsule. Think about which way blood flows - in through one vessel, out through the other to the rest of the kidney.
Look inside the cup-shaped capsule for the tangled ball of tiny vessels where filtration happens. Think about what name is given to that knot of capillaries.
Focus on the thin inner wall of the capsule that wraps tightly around that capillary knot. Think about which specialised cells with finger-like processes form that layer.
walkthrough:
Sorting Out Blood In and Blood Out**
Blood arrives at the glomerulus through the afferent arteriole and leaves through the efferent arteriole. The efferent vessel has a smaller diameter, which helps build up high hydrostatic pressure for filtration. In Fig. 6.1 the vessel on the left is the outgoing, narrower one, so that is E.

Spotting the Filter**
Inside the double-walled cup you can see a mass of looping vessels. That is not a single vessel, it is a knot of fenestrated capillaries where plasma is forced out. That whole knot is the glomerulus, so that is G.

Finding the Podocytes**
The Bowman's capsule has an outer parietal layer and an inner visceral layer that hugs the capillaries. That inner layer is made of podocytes with pedicels that wrap around capillaries and form filtration slits. So P points to that inner epithelium lining the capsular space around the glomerulus.

Final answer: E - label line to the narrower vessel on the left at the top of the capsule (efferent arteriole); G - label line to the knot of capillaries inside the capsule (glomerulus); P - label line to the inner epithelium of the capsule surrounding the capillaries (podocyte layer).

hints: Think about what selective reabsorption needs to do - take back all glucose, amino acids, most ions and water from a large volume of filtrate very quickly.
Recall the general rule that absorbing cells increase their apical surface area. What finger-like projections would you expect on the side facing the tubule lumen?
Many solutes are moved against a concentration gradient by cotransport linked to sodium. What organelle must be abundant to supply ATP for this?
Think about the proteins sitting in the cell surface membranes that actually carry solutes and water across.
Think about how the cell keeps reabsorbed fluid moving in one direction toward the blood and prevents leakage back between cells.
walkthrough:
Increasing Uptake Area**
The apical membrane facing the filtrate is folded into dense microvilli, the brush border. This hugely increases surface area, so glucose, amino acids, ions and water can be reabsorbed rapidly by diffusion and carrier-mediated transport.

Powering Active Uptake**
PCT cells contain very many mitochondria. They generate ATP by aerobic respiration for the sodium-potassium pumps in the basal and lateral membranes. This maintains a steep sodium gradient that drives sodium-coupled cotransport of glucose and amino acids into the cell.

Providing Transport Routes**
The membranes contain many transport proteins - sodium-glucose cotransporters, amino acid cotransporters, ion pumps and channels - plus aquaporins for osmosis. The basal membrane is highly folded / infolded to house many of these pumps and to increase area for exit of solutes toward the interstitial fluid and capillaries.

Keeping Flow One-Way**
Adjacent PCT cells are joined near the lumen by tight junctions. This seals the gaps between cells so filtrate cannot leak back, ensuring reabsorbed substances must pass through the cells and then out to the blood.

Final answer: PCT cells have: microvilli / brush border to increase surface area for absorption; many mitochondria to provide ATP for active transport; many carrier / cotransporter proteins and Na+/K+ pumps for uptake of glucose, amino acids and ions; aquaporins for water reabsorption; infolded basal membrane to increase area for transport out to blood; tight junctions between cells to prevent back-leak.

hints: Think about where in the brain water potential is sensed. Special receptor cells shrink or swell as blood becomes more or less concentrated.
Recall the hormone made by hypothalamic neurones when blood is too concentrated. Think about its effect - it makes the kidney retain water, so anti-diuresis.
Think about where that hypothalamic hormone is stored and released from into the blood - it is not the anterior lobe that makes other tropic hormones.
Think about the general control pattern where a change triggers a response that reverses the original change back to the set point.
walkthrough:
Detecting Blood Concentration**
Cells called osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus constantly monitor the water potential of the blood. When water potential falls, water leaves these cells by osmosis and they shrink, which stimulates the hypothalamus.

Releasing the Water-Conserving Hormone**
The hypothalamic neurones increase production of ADH, antidiuretic hormone, also called vasopressin. ADH travels down axons and is released into the blood from the posterior pituitary gland.

Restoring Balance by Negative Feedback**
ADH increases water reabsorption in the collecting duct, so more concentrated urine is produced and blood water potential rises back to the set point. As the set point is restored, ADH secretion is switched down. Because the response reverses the original stimulus, this is negative feedback homeostasis.
Final answer: osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus; ADH / antidiuretic hormone / vasopressin; posterior pituitary (gland); negative feedback.
